claim: Distributions of spontaneous population firing rates are subject to accurate homeostatic control following increase of synaptic inhibition in cultured hippocampal networks.
source: In this study, we show that distributions of spontaneous population firing rates and synchrony are subject to accurate homeostatic control following increase of synaptic inhibition in cultured hippocampal networks.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including MEA recordings and calcium imaging.

claim: Distributions of spontaneous population synchrony are subject to accurate homeostatic control following increase of synaptic inhibition in cultured hippocampal networks.
source: In this study, we show that distributions of spontaneous population firing rates and synchrony are subject to accurate homeostatic control following increase of synaptic inhibition in cultured hippocampal networks.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data on burst patterns and synchrony measurements.

claim: Reduction in firing rate triggered synaptic adaptive responses operating as global homeostatic mechanisms to maintain firing macro-stability.
source: Reduction in firing rate triggered synaptic and intrinsic adaptive responses operating as global homeostatic mechanisms to maintain firing macro-stability, without achieving local homeostasis at the single-neuron level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in mEPSC frequency and amplitude, and release probability following baclofen application.

claim: Reduction in firing rate triggered intrinsic adaptive responses operating as global homeostatic mechanisms to maintain firing macro-stability.
source: Reduction in firing rate triggered synaptic and intrinsic adaptive responses operating as global homeostatic mechanisms to maintain firing macro-stability, without achieving local homeostasis at the single-neuron level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in resting membrane potential, input resistance, and F-I curves following baclofen application.

claim: Homeostatic mechanisms do not achieve local homeostasis at the single-neuron level.
source: Reduction in firing rate triggered synaptic and intrinsic adaptive responses operating as global homeostatic mechanisms to maintain firing macro-stability, without achieving local homeostasis at the single-neuron level.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that only 11% of units returned to baseline firing rates after baclofen application, while 89% changed significantly.

claim: Adaptive mechanisms reduced short-term facilitation essential for synaptic discrimination of input patterns.
source: Adaptive mechanisms, while stabilizing population firing properties, reduced short-term facilitation essential for synaptic discrimination of input patterns.
evidence: This is supported by FM dye imaging data showing that short-term synaptic facilitation was decreased from 1.9- to 1.2-fold after 4 hr and was completely abolished following 2 days of baclofen incubation.

claim: Invariant ongoing population dynamics emerge from intrinsically unstable activity patterns of individual neurons and synapses.
source: Thus, invariant ongoing population dynamics emerge from intrinsically unstable activity patterns of individual neurons and synapses.
evidence: This is supported by data showing stable population firing rates despite variable single-unit firing rates, and changes in synaptic properties.

claim: Only 25% of CA1 cells with place fields at one recording session exhibited the same properties 5 days later in freely moving mice.
source: That study, performed by monitoring Ca2+ dynamics in thousands of CA1 cells over weeks through a miniature head-mounted microscope, revealed a remarkable degree of instability in the coding of space: only 25% of cells with place fields at one recording session exhibited the same properties 5 days later.
evidence: This claim is attributed to a previous study (Ziv et al., 2013) and is cited as background information.

claim: Diverse activity patterns at the single-neuron level gave rise to largely invariant spatial representations at the population level in CA1 hippocampal neurons.
source: Importantly, the diverse activity patterns at the single-neuron level gave rise to largely invariant spatial representations at the population level.
evidence: This claim refers to findings from a previous study (Ziv et al., 2013) and is cited as background information.

claim: GABABRs mediate presynaptic inhibition via inhibition of presynaptic calcium transients.
source: GABABRs mediate presynaptic inhibition via inhibition of presynaptic calcium transients (Wu and Saggau, 1995; Laviv et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GABABR-mediated inhibition is frequency-dependent.
source: As GABABR-mediated inhibition is frequency-dependent (Varela et al., 1997; Kreitzer and Regehr, 2000; Ohliger-Frerking et al., 2003), we quantified the effects of baclofen for two types of input: low-frequency single spikes (30 stimuli at 1 Hz) and high-frequency spike bursts (30 stimuli delivered as 6 bursts; each burst contains 5 stimuli at 100 Hz), while maintaining the mean spiking rate constant at 1 Hz (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and is confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Baclofen inhibits synaptic vesicle release, displaying preferential effects during low-frequency stimulation.
source: As expected, baclofen inhibits synaptic vesicle release, displaying preferential effects during low-frequency stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM1-43 dye imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IC50 for single spikes was approximately 23-fold lower than for bursts (0.33 and 7.6 μM, respectively).
source: Quantitatively, IC50 for single spikes was ∼23-fold lower than for bursts (0.33 and 7.6 μM, respectively, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Short-term facilitation was enhanced in a wide range of baclofen concentrations (0.01–10 μM).
source: As a result, short-term facilitation was enhanced in a wide range of baclofen concentrations (0.01–10 μM, Figure 1C), indicating a conversion of synapses to a high-pass filter mode.
evidence: This claim is supported by FM method data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Acute baclofen application converts synapses to a high-pass filter mode.
source: As a result, short-term facilitation was enhanced in a wide range of baclofen concentrations (0.01–10 μM, Figure 1C), indicating a conversion of synapses to a high-pass filter mode.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing enhanced short-term facilitation.

claim: Baclofen caused a fast and robust drop in single-unit firing rates.
source: As expected, baclofen caused a fast and robust drop in single-unit firing rates (Figure 1F,G), leading to a reduction of the population mean firing rate to 25 ± 4% (1 µM baclofen, see raster plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and to 1.2 ± 0.4% (10 µM baclofen) of baseline values (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by MEA recording data shown in Figures 1F, 1G, and 1H.

claim: 1 µM baclofen reduced population mean firing rate to 25 ± 4% of baseline values.
source: As expected, baclofen caused a fast and robust drop in single-unit firing rates (Figure 1F,G), leading to a reduction of the population mean firing rate to 25 ± 4% (1 µM baclofen, see raster plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and to 1.2 ± 0.4% (10 µM baclofen) of baseline values (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by MEA recording data.

claim: 10 µM baclofen reduced population mean firing rate to 1.2 ± 0.4% of baseline values.
source: As expected, baclofen caused a fast and robust drop in single-unit firing rates (Figure 1F,G), leading to a reduction of the population mean firing rate to 25 ± 4% (1 µM baclofen, see raster plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and to 1.2 ± 0.4% (10 µM baclofen) of baseline values (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by MEA recording data.

claim: Unit firing rates were highly heterogeneous and skewed towards low frequencies.
source: Unit firing rates were highly heterogeneous and skewed towards low frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as has been previously reported in vivo (Mizuseki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and is consistent with previous in vivo studies.

claim: Baclofen caused a fast and pronounced drop in firing rates to 1.2 ± 0.4% of baseline values.
source: As expected, baclofen caused a fast and pronounced drop in firing rates to 1.2 ± 0.4% of baseline values (Figure 2A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MEA recording data shown in Figures 2A, 2C, and 2D.

claim: Firing rates gradually returned to baseline values, reaching 57 ± 8% and 103 ± 14% of baseline after 1 and 2 days, respectively.
source: Indeed, firing rates gradually returned to baseline values, reaching 57 ± 8% and 103 ± 14% of baseline after 1 and 2 days, respectively (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term MEA recording data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The average firing rates of networks under control conditions showed changes of similar magnitude during two recording days (113 ± 9% of baseline after 2 days).
source: Notably, the average firing rates of networks under control conditions showed changes of similar magnitude during two recording days (without baclofen application, 113 ± 9% of baseline after 2 days; Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by control MEA recording data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: The characteristic log-normal distributions of single-unit firing patterns were essentially identical before and 2 days after baclofen application.
source: Moreover, the characteristic log-normal distributions of single-unit firing patterns were essentially identical before and 2 days after baclofen application (Figure 2E, p = 0.66; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: This claim is supported by distribution analysis shown in Figure 2E with statistical testing.

claim: Baclofen remains potent after over 2 days of exposure to recording conditions.
source: Importantly, baclofen remains potent after over 2 days of exposure to recording conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that pre-incubated baclofen retains its activity.

claim: Washout of baclofen following 2 days caused a significant increase in firing rate.
source: Additionally, washout of baclofen following 2 days caused a significant increase in firing rate, indicating sustained activity of both baclofen and the GABABR-induced G-protein-mediated signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by washout experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: GABABRs did not undergo desensitization under experimental conditions.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of the GABABR-mediated presynaptic inhibition, as measured by FM dyes, was not reduced following washout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F), indicating that GABABRs did not undergo desensitization under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by FM dye imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Only 23 ± 3% of units remained significantly unchanged during 2 days of control recordings, while 77 ± 3% changed their firing rates significantly.
source: Only 23 ± 3% of units remained significantly unchanged during 2 days of control recordings, while 77 ± 3% changed their firing rates significantly (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit analysis data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The change in firing rate after 2 days of recordings was negatively correlated with the initial firing rate of the same unit under both control and baclofen conditions.
source: The change in firing rate after 2 days of recordings was negatively correlated with the initial firing rate of the same unit under both control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Spearman r = −0.29, p < 0.0001, n = 490) and baclofen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Spearman r = −0.47, p < 0.0001, n = 305) conditions, due to a larger relative variability of low firing units.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The mean movement of neurons (1.6 ± 0.1 μM) was negligible in comparison to the size of the electrode (30 µM) and neuron's cell body (11.4 ± 0.3 µM).
source: To ensure that per unit variability is not due to a possible movement of neurons in and out from recording electrodes, we measured the movement of individual neurons over the course of 2 days and found that the mean movement of neurons (1.6 ± 0.1 μM) was negligible in comparison to the size of the electrode (30 µM) and neuron's cell body (11.4 ± 0.3 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of neuronal movement.

claim: Single spikes induced robust calcium transients (24.6 ± 1.4% ΔF/F).
source: Single spikes induced robust calcium transients (24.6 ± 1.4% ΔF/F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High-frequency bursts consisting of 2–10 spikes at 100 Hz induced significantly higher ΔF/F peak amplitudes as compared with single spikes.
source: Although the exact number of spikes could not be accurately predicted from the size of the calcium transients, high-frequency bursts consisting of 2–10 spikes at 100 Hz induced significantly higher ΔF/F peak amplitudes as compared with single spikes and the average ΔF/F linearly correlated with the number of spikes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The average ΔF/F linearly correlated with the number of spikes.
source: Although the exact number of spikes could not be accurately predicted from the size of the calcium transients, high-frequency bursts consisting of 2–10 spikes at 100 Hz induced significantly higher ΔF/F peak amplitudes as compared with single spikes and the average ΔF/F linearly correlated with the number of spikes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 10 μM baclofen blocked Ca2+ transients acutely.
source: Analysis of Ca2+ dynamics in 192 neurons shows that 10 μM baclofen blocked Ca2+ transients acutely, while 48 hr after baclofen incubation the mean Ca2+-transient amplitude returned to the baseline level (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: 48 hr after baclofen incubation the mean Ca2+-transient amplitude returned to the baseline level.
source: Analysis of Ca2+ dynamics in 192 neurons shows that 10 μM baclofen blocked Ca2+ transients acutely, while 48 hr after baclofen incubation the mean Ca2+-transient amplitude returned to the baseline level (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: 54 ± 6% of neurons did not return to their baseline values 2 days after baclofen application.
source: Despite stability of Ca2+ dynamics at the population level, 54 ± 6% of neurons did not return to their baseline values 2 days after baclofen application (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-neuron calcium imaging analysis shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Baclofen transiently increased population firing synchrony by increasing the fraction of spikes participating in bursts.
source: Baclofen transiently increased population firing synchrony by increasing the fraction of spikes participating in bursts, burst duration (Figure 4B,C), and number of spikes per network burst (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by burst analysis data shown in Figures 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The observed GABABR-mediated increase in firing synchrony returned to baseline values after 14 hr.
source: The observed GABABR-mediated increase in firing synchrony returned to baseline values after 14 hr (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Under control conditions, 42 ± 2% of units significantly changed the fraction of spikes in bursts, while 56 ± 2% remained unchanged.
source: Under control conditions, 42 ± 2% of units significantly changed the fraction of spikes in bursts, while 56 ± 2% remained unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit burst analysis.

claim: 2 days after baclofen application, 63 ± 8% of units were significantly changed in burst patterns, while only 37 ± 8% of units remained unchanged.
source: 2 days after baclofen application, 63 ± 8% were significantly changed, while only 37 ± 8% of units remained unchanged (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit burst analysis shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Acute application of baclofen almost completely blocked both sEPSCs and sIPSCs.
source: As expected, acute application of baclofen almost completely blocked both sEPSCs and sIPSCs, from 0.40 ± 0.07 and 0.87 ± 0.1 nS to 0.02 ± 0.006 and 0.06 ± 0.02 nS for GE and GI, respectively (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: After 4 hr of incubation with baclofen, GE and GI partially recovered to 0.16 ± 0.07 nS and 0.61 ± 0.2 nS, respectively.
source: After 4 hr of incubation with baclofen, GE and GI partially recovered to 0.16 ± 0.07 nS and 0.61 ± 0.2 nS, respectively (Figure 5C,D), suggesting a faster rate of GI homeostatic regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: After 2 days in the presence of baclofen, GE reached 0.44 ± 0.1 nS and GI reached 1.02 ± 0.2 nS.
source: Finally, after 2 days in the presence of baclofen, the network showed full recovery with GE reaching 0.44 ± 0.1 nS and GI reaching 1.02 ± 0.2 nS (p > 0.8, Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: I/E ratio was transiently increased from 3.1 ± 0.4 to 9.9 ± 2.8 following 4 hr baclofen incubation.
source: As a result, I/E ratio was transiently increased from 3.1 ± 0.4 to 9.9 ± 2.8 following 4 hr baclofen incubation (p < 0.001), returning to the baseline levels following 2 days of baclofen (3.04 ± 0.5, p > 0.5; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by I/E ratio analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: I/E ratio returned to the baseline levels following 2 days of baclofen (3.04 ± 0.5).
source: As a result, I/E ratio was transiently increased from 3.1 ± 0.4 to 9.9 ± 2.8 following 4 hr baclofen incubation (p < 0.001), returning to the baseline levels following 2 days of baclofen (3.04 ± 0.5, p > 0.5; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by I/E ratio analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Acute baclofen application did not have a significant effect on mEPSCs.
source: While acute baclofen application did not have a significant effect on mEPSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) as has been reported previously (Lei and McBain, 2003), chronic baclofen incubation triggered gradual changes in mEPSC frequency and amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSC recording data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: A 1.25-fold increase in mEPSC amplitude to 30.8 ± 2.2 pA was detected 2 days following baclofen application.
source: However, a 1.25-fold increase to 30.8 ± 2.2 pA (p < 0.05) was detected 2 days following baclofen application (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSC amplitude analysis shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: mEPSC frequency increased twofold from 2.1 ± 0.7 to 4.3 ± 1.5 Hz following 4 hr baclofen application.
source: This was coupled with twofold increase in the frequency of mEPSCs from 2.1 ± 0.7 to 4.3 ± 1.5 Hz (p < 0.05) following 4 hr baclofen application and a large 4.8-fold increase to 10 ± 3.2 Hz (p < 0.01) following 2 days (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSC frequency analysis shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: mEPSC frequency increased 4.8-fold to 10 ± 3.2 Hz following 2 days baclofen application.
source: This was coupled with twofold increase in the frequency of mEPSCs from 2.1 ± 0.7 to 4.3 ± 1.5 Hz (p < 0.05) following 4 hr baclofen application and a large 4.8-fold increase to 10 ± 3.2 Hz (p < 0.01) following 2 days (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSC frequency analysis shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Resting membrane potential was −64.8 ± 1.7 mV in untreated neurons, became more depolarized after 4 hr (−58.2 ± 2.2 mV), and further depolarized after 2 days (−55.4 ± 1.5 mV).
source: Additionally, resting membrane potential (RMP, Figure 7C) was −64.8 ± 1.7 mV in untreated neurons, became more depolarized already after 4 hr (−58.2 ± 2.2, p < 0.05) and further depolarized after 2 days (−55.4 ± 1.5 mV, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recording data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Input resistance was significantly increased following 2 days baclofen incubation (from 233 ± 14 to 373 ± 59 MΩ).
source: Finally, input resistance (Rin), determined by the voltage response to increasing somatic current injections ranging from −80 to −20 pA, showed a tendency towards larger values after 4 hr and was significantly increased following 2 days baclofen incubation (from 233 ± 14 to 373 ± 59 MΩ, p < 0.01; Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by input resistance measurements shown in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: There was a 1.5- and 1.8-fold increase in ΔF across synaptic populations following 4 hr and 2 days of baclofen incubation, respectively.
source: Our results demonstrate a 1.5- and 1.8-fold increase in ΔF across synaptic populations following 4 hr and 2 days, respectively (p < 0.001, Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM1-43 dye imaging data shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: The destaining rate constant increased by approximately 36% following 2 days of baclofen incubation.
source: The destaining rate constant (measured as 1/τdecay, where τdecay is an exponential time course) increased by ∼36% following 2 days of baclofen incubation (p < 0.01; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM destaining rate analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Short-term synaptic facilitation was decreased from 1.9- to 1.2-fold after 4 hr of baclofen incubation.
source: Indeed, short-term synaptic facilitation was decreased from 1.9- to 1.2-fold after 4 hr (p < 0.001, Figure 8D,E) and was completely abolished following 2 days (p < 0.001, Figure 8D,E) of incubation with baclofen.
evidence: This claim is supported by short-term plasticity analysis shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Short-term synaptic facilitation was completely abolished following 2 days of incubation with baclofen.
source: Indeed, short-term synaptic facilitation was decreased from 1.9- to 1.2-fold after 4 hr (p < 0.001, Figure 8D,E) and was completely abolished following 2 days (p < 0.001, Figure 8D,E) of incubation with baclofen.
evidence: This claim is supported by short-term plasticity analysis shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: CNQX (10 µM) caused a reduction in the population mean firing rate to 52 ± 12% of baseline values immediately after application.
source: CNQX (10 µM) caused a reduction in the population mean firing rate to 52 ± 12% of baseline values immediately after application (p < 0.01; Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MEA recording data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Application of NMDAR and AMPAR blockers together resulted in approximately 80% of firing rate inhibition.
source: Application of NMDAR and AMPAR blockers together resulted in ∼80% of firing rate inhibition (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that NMDARs contribute ∼30% to spontaneous spiking activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: NMDARs contribute approximately 30% to spontaneous spiking activity.
source: Application of NMDAR and AMPAR blockers together resulted in ∼80% of firing rate inhibition (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that NMDARs contribute ∼30% to spontaneous spiking activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between CNQX alone (52% reduction) and CNQX+AP5 together (80% reduction).

claim: The population mean firing rate remained largely uncompensated after CNQX application, staying at 40 ± 5% of baseline 2 days following the perturbation.
source: While CNQX triggered a compensatory increase in synapse release probability already 4 hr after its application (Figure 9F,G and (Jakawich et al., 2010)), the population mean firing rate remained largely uncompensated, staying at 40 ± 5% of baseline 2 days following the perturbation (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term MEA recording data shown in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: Only 16 ± 8% of units remained significantly unchanged during 2 days of CNQX perturbation, while 71 ± 8% decreased their firing rates.
source: When examining changes at the individual unit level, we found that only 16 ± 8% of units remained significantly unchanged during 2 days of the perturbation, while 71 ± 8% decreased their firing rates (p < 0.001, Figure 9D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit analysis shown in Figures 9D and 9E.

claim: CNQX caused a permanent reduction in the fraction of spikes participating in population bursts.
source: Analysis of firing pattern shows that CNQX caused a permanent reduction in the fraction of spikes participating in population bursts (Figure 9A,H), as well as in the number of spikes comprising population bursts (Figure 9—figure supplement 3A), reflecting a reduction in firing synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by burst analysis data shown in Figures 9A, 9H, and Figure 9—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Homeostatic control systems are equally precise at the level of individual neurons and neuronal populations.
source: Second, are homeostatic control systems equally precise at the level of individual neurons and neuronal populations?
evidence: This is a research question posed in the introduction, and the manuscript data shows that homeostatic control is NOT equally precise at different levels, with population-level control being more precise than single-neuron level.

claim: The observed differences in the precision of homeostatic control at different spatial scales challenge cell-autonomous theory of network homeostasis.
source: The observed differences in the precision of homeostatic control at different spatial scales challenge cell-autonomous theory of network homeostasis and suggest the existence of network-wide regulation rules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing greater stability at population level compared to single-neuron level.

claim: The observed differences in the precision of homeostatic control at different spatial scales suggest the existence of network-wide regulation rules.
source: The observed differences in the precision of homeostatic control at different spatial scales challenge cell-autonomous theory of network homeostasis and suggest the existence of network-wide regulation rules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing greater stability at population level compared to single-neuron level.

claim: Neuronal circuits achieve an ongoing balance between flexibility and stability to enable plastic adaptations to environmental changes, while maintaining neuronal activity in a stable regime over extended timescales.
source: Neural circuits achieve an ongoing balance between flexibility and stability to enable plastic adaptations to environmental changes, while maintaining neuronal activity in a stable regime over extended timescales.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural circuit function supported by the literature and the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Diverse homeostatic negative feedback systems operate to stabilize ongoing spiking properties in neuronal populations around a predefined 'set point' in face of constant environmental changes.
source: Diverse homeostatic negative feedback systems operate to stabilize ongoing spiking properties in neuronal populations around a predefined 'set point' in face of constant environmental changes (Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004; Davis, 2006; Marder and Goaillard, 2006).
evidence: This is a general statement about homeostatic mechanisms supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chronic AMPAR blockade increases both the frequency and the amplitude of mEPSCs.
source: While previous studies demonstrated that chronic AMPAR blockade increases both the frequency and the amplitude of mEPSCs (Thiagarajan et al., 2002) already 4 hr after application of the antagonist (Jakawich et al., 2010), its effect on firing properties of the network has not been explored yet.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both pre- and postsynaptic modifications of quantal excitatory synaptic transmission occur following chronic, use-dependent inhibition of the evoked synaptic activity.
source: These data indicate that both pre- and postsynaptic modifications of quantal excitatory synaptic transmission occur following chronic, use-dependent inhibition of the evoked synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mEPSC data showing increases in both amplitude (postsynaptic) and frequency (presynaptic).

claim: Increased intrinsic excitability contributes to the homeostatic restoration of network firing properties following chronic GABABR-mediated inhibition.
source: These data show that, in addition to synaptic modifications, increased intrinsic excitability contributes to the homeostatic restoration of network firing properties following chronic GABABR-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the F-I curve, RMP, and input resistance data.

claim: An increase in the release probability of hippocampal boutons constitutes an adaptive mechanism stabilizing firing properties of hippocampal network.
source: Thus, an increase in the release probability of hippocampal boutons constitutes an adaptive mechanism stabilizing firing properties of hippocampal network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FM dye imaging data showing increased ΔF and destaining rate.

claim: Homeostasis of mean firing rate is expected to be paralleled by concurrent changes in short-term synaptic plasticity given an inverse correlation between release probability and short-term synaptic facilitation.
source: Given an inverse correlation between release probability and short-term synaptic facilitation (Debanne et al., 1996; Dobrunz and Stevens, 1997), homeostasis of mean firing rate is expected to be paralleled by concurrent changes in short-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established knowledge about the relationship between release probability and short-term plasticity, supported by citations.

claim: Short-term synaptic plasticity is not preserved under homeostasis of population firing properties.
source: These results demonstrate that short-term synaptic plasticity is not preserved under homeostasis of population firing properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing abolishment of short-term facilitation after 2 days of baclofen incubation.

claim: Firing rates and patterns are independently regulated.
source: Based on these results, we may conclude that (1) firing rates and patterns are independently regulated; (2) homeostatic systems generally sense a drop in spiking rates to induce an adaptive increase in excitatory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of baclofen and CNQX, which both reduce firing rates but have opposite effects on synchrony.

claim: Homeostatic systems generally sense a drop in spiking rates to induce an adaptive increase in excitatory synaptic transmission.
source: Based on these results, we may conclude that (1) firing rates and patterns are independently regulated; (2) homeostatic systems generally sense a drop in spiking rates to induce an adaptive increase in excitatory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that both baclofen and CNQX trigger similar synaptic adaptations despite different effects on synchrony.

claim: Adaptations at the level of intrinsic neuronal excitability and inhibitory drive are not sufficient to compensate the blockade of AMPAR-mediated excitatory drive.
source: Thus, our results indicate that adaptations at the level of intrinsic neuronal excitability and inhibitory drive are not sufficient to compensate the blockade of AMPAR-mediated excitatory drive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that firing rates did not recover after CNQX application despite synaptic adaptations.

claim: Similar network properties may arise from multiple configurations of individual components.
source: These results highlight the idea that similar network properties may arise from multiple configurations of individual components (Prinz et al., 2004; Marder and Goaillard, 2006).
evidence: This is a general principle supported by citations and confirmed by the experimental findings showing variable single-unit properties giving rise to stable population properties.

claim: Population firing homeostasis is more than a sum of single-neuron adaptive responses.
source: Most importantly, the observed differences in the precision of homeostatic regulation at different spatial scales suggest that population firing homeostasis is more than a sum of single-neuron adaptive responses, implying the existence of network-wide regulation rules (Maffei and Fontanini, 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that population-level homeostasis is more precise than single-neuron level homeostasis.

claim: Robust homeostatic control of ongoing population dynamics may coexist with unstable short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, robust homeostatic control of ongoing population dynamics may coexist with unstable short-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that population firing rates are restored while short-term facilitation is abolished.

claim: Impairments of short-term synaptic plasticity and working memory functions, characterizing initial phases of numerous brain disorders, may be the tradeoff resulting from the system's efforts to maintain phenotypic stability of spontaneous population firing patterns.
source: Thus, impairments of short-term synaptic plasticity and working memory functions, characterizing initial phases of numerous brain disorders, may be the tradeoff resulting from the system's efforts to maintain phenotypic stability of spontaneous population firing patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about the tradeoff between population stability and short-term plasticity.

claim: Primary cultures of CA3–CA1 hippocampal neurons were prepared from newborn BALB/c mice on postnatal days 0–2.
source: Primary cultures of CA3–CA1 hippocampal neurons were prepared from newborn BALB/c mice on postnatal days 0–2, as described (Slutsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental preparation.

claim: The experiments were performed in 15–22 DIV cultures.
source: The experiments were performed in 15–22 DIV cultures.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the timing of experiments.

claim: Cultures were plated on MEA plates containing 59 TiN recording and one internal reference electrodes.
source: Cultures were plated on MEA plates containing 59 TiN recording and one internal reference electrodes (Multi Channel Systems [MCS], Germany).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the recording setup.

claim: Electrodes are 30 µm in diameter and spaced 500 µm apart.
source: Electrodes are 30 µm in diameter and spaced 500 µm apart.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the electrode specifications.

claim: GCaMP6f displays single-action-potential sensitivity and broad dynamic range.
source: We utilized the genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator GCaMP6f that displays single-action-potential sensitivity and broad dynamic range (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a property of GCaMP6f supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: An AAV-based gene delivery system under the synapsin promoter was used to express GCaMP6f in hippocampal neurons.
source: An AAV-based gene delivery system under the synapsin promoter was used to express GCaMP6f in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the expression system.

claim: Hippocampal cultures were infected by AAV2/1-Syn-GCaMP6f at 5–8 day in vitro.
source: Hippocampal cultures were infected by AAV2/1-Syn-GCaMP6f at 5–8 day in vitro.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the timing of infection.

claim: The experiments were performed 8–12 days post-infection when expression reached stable levels.
source: The experiments were performed 8–12 days post-infection when expression reached stable levels.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the timing of experiments relative to infection.
